This aid accompanies the October 2026 course. Before a selection, confirm the current agreement, agency procedures and any relevant court orders with Human Resources.

Remember. Establish job-related criteria before reviewing candidates and apply them consistently. Do not use race, sex, disability or another protected trait as a substitute for evidence of qualifications. Follow applicable nondiscrimination, accommodation and selection requirements. Raise any conflicting direction with Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer, and preserve an accurate decision record.

Before posting. Ask Human Resources which agreement and vacancy provisions apply. MAPE Article 16 addresses posting, interest bids, seniority-unit layoff lists, claiming and other appointment methods, with eligibility rules and exceptions; the summary is not an unconditional sequence for every vacancy. Use the position description to set a manageable set of criteria and scoring anchors. Date them and examine whether each requirement is necessary for the work. Describe language skills and intercultural work as observable capabilities, not identity proxies. Do not use learning reflections or results from this app to rank candidates.

Reaching people. Share recruitment information widely, including through disability and community networks and in greater Minnesota. Make selection opportunities available under the applicable eligibility rules. Include the accommodation notice and promptly route requests through the responsible process. Provide consistent information in accessible formats.

The interview. Use consistent core questions, job-related scoring criteria and neutral follow-ups. Arrange required accommodations; identical timing or format is not always equitable access. Ask about the work and the ability to perform its duties, rather than seeking irrelevant personal information. Route accommodation questions through Human Resources or the ADA coordinator, and do not independently seek medical details. Evaluate relevant evidence rather than accent, manner or vague impressions of fit. Score independently before discussing the evidence together.

The decision. Compare the evidence against the established criteria and record the reason for the selection. If a direction appears to conflict with those criteria or nondiscrimination requirements, ask Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer to resolve it before proceeding. Provide any required justification from accurate, dated records. Preserve the original criteria, scores and reasons; document corrections transparently rather than rewriting the record to defend a result. Follow applicable retention and preservation requirements.
Use this dated guide to distinguish legal and policy duties from enforcement guidance, and to identify what needs current confirmation before you act.

Remember. This is general information, not legal advice or a substitute for official agency direction. Learning in this app does not satisfy required state training. Confirm assigned training and applicable duties through the agency’s designated process. A secondary report can help locate a development, but check the underlying rule, order or official guidance before relying on it.

Apply current policy. Under Policies 1436 and 1329, managers and supervisors must immediately report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination, including sexual harassment, to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Promptly forward accommodation requests and tell the requester who will decide. Under Policy 1433, supervisors must not request medical information from someone seeking an accommodation; the ADA coordinator handles any appropriate documentation request. Complete assigned state training. Ames rejects a heightened evidentiary burden for majority-group Title VII claimants. Muldrow concerns discriminatory job transfers: harm to an employment term or condition need not be significant. These holdings do not replace review of the facts and applicable requirements.

Understand enforcement guidance. The EEOC’s March 2025 technical assistance addresses discrimination in hiring, training, mentoring and other employment opportunities. The DOJ’s July 29, 2025 funding-recipient guidance identifies non-binding best practices; OMB M-25-33 directs federal agencies to follow that guidance in administering federal programs. Distinguish those agency positions from statutes and court rulings. Have the responsible legal or Human Resources office review program-specific implications, including participation criteria and retaliation protections, rather than treating a course summary as a legal determination.

When rules or litigation change. Identify the exact law, regulation, order or guidance, its date, the people or programs it covers, and what the agency has directed staff to do. A change in federal enforcement does not by itself establish that a state duty has ended. For United States v. Minnesota, obtain the current case status and any operative orders through Human Resources or legal counsel. Do not repeat an earlier statement that no court has ruled as though it were a current finding.

Accessibility dates to confirm. DOJ’s current Title II web-rule guidance lists April 26, 2027 for state and local entities with populations of 50,000 or more. HHS’s May 7, 2026 announcement lists May 11, 2027 for covered recipients with 15 or more employees. These dates concern specified web and mobile accessibility standards; they do not suspend existing access duties or state accessibility requirements. Confirm the rule’s scope and current agency implementation schedule. Obtain litigation deadlines from the current docket or responsible legal office rather than this aid.

Do next. Before an assignment, schedule change or hiring decision, identify the relevant criteria and any required review. Keep current Human Resources, Affirmative Action Officer, ADA coordinator and labor-relations contacts available. Set a proportionate review date for changing guidance, and act sooner when a new requirement or concern calls for it.
Connect learning to supervisory decisions, examine what the evidence supports, and choose how to review the effects of your practice.

Remember. Learning can inform a decision, but completion alone does not show that practice or outcomes improved. This program does not offer training credits. Optional learning supports DHS responsibilities under the Equity Policy, including applicable equity-analysis requirements and assigned agency training. Complete required training through the agency’s designated process. Follow the privacy notice for the feature you use, and keep confidential personnel or case information in authorized work systems.

What the evidence supports. Bezrukova and colleagues’ 2016 meta-analysis found stronger effects on knowledge and training reactions than on attitudes or behavior, with results varying by design and context. Chang and colleagues’ 2019 trial at one organization found different attitude and behavior effects across groups. Neither establishes that completing a course improves outcomes in a particular DHS unit. Use clear criteria, accountable decisions and feedback, then examine what actually happens rather than assuming a tool or training is effective.

Where supervisors influence equity. Examine access to your time and support; the distribution of visible and routine work; the evidence used in ratings and hiring; how requests and reports are handled; and whether staff can participate in meetings. Identify which decisions you control and which require another role or process.

Four habits. Establish relevant criteria before deciding. Keep required records in the appropriate system. Invite feedback through consistent, accessible questions about the work. Review the evidence and decide whether to retain a sound practice, address a barrier or seek further review.

Watch for unsupported conclusions. A completed course does not prove that a concern has been addressed. An average can conceal different experiences. Records written after a decision may miss how it was reached. One person’s account should be heard without treating that person as a representative of an entire group.

Do next. Choose a decision or practice within your role. Identify the evidence, the responsible people, any required process and when its effects should be reviewed. If you use a fictional example for optional learning, keep it separate from official records. For real work, follow applicable duties and review timing rather than treating a fixed practice interval as a requirement.

The Intercultural Development Inventory is a licensed assessment administered by an IDI Qualified Administrator. This program explains its developmental framework but does not administer the assessment, reproduce protected material, or use individual results for employment decisions or access to learning.

Purpose and model: the IDI places results along the Intercultural Development Continuum, whose five orientations are Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. Integration belongs to Bennett's separate Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity, where it concerns identity across cultural worldviews. Community participation in service design is a program practice; it is not a sixth IDI orientation or an assessment result.

Evidence: review the publisher's research and validation material alongside relevant independent studies. Consider the population, methods, uses and limitations of each study before drawing a conclusion about a particular setting.

Interpretation: the publisher describes individual and group reports as snapshots of an approach to cultural differences and commonalities. Individual results are discussed with a licensed Qualified Administrator. A result is not a judgment of character or a complete account of workplace behavior; this program does not use it for hiring, promotion or performance evaluation.

Program use: learn about the framework, consider questions for development, and seek qualified administration if an assessment is appropriate. This program does not administer, score, store or interpret individual results. It does not reproduce protected assessment material. Learning and reflection can begin without taking an assessment.

Implicit-association tasks examine associations through response patterns such as reaction times. A single result does not establish someone's character or reliably predict a specific action. This program links to these resources for optional reflection and does not use individual results for workplace decisions.

Purpose: compare the relative ease of associating concepts, evaluations or stereotypes. Implicit and explicitly reported attitudes may differ; the task does not establish whether a person consciously endorses an association.

Evidence and limits: Project Implicit describes continuing debate about repeated scores and behavioral prediction. The publisher reports associations with behavior in aggregate, while cautioning against predictions about one person on one occasion. It also cautions against treating one result as a permanent personal characteristic. Use the result as a question for reflection, not a diagnosis.

Program use: optional reflection without submitting or discussing individual results here. External research sites have their own participation and data-handling terms; read those before deciding whether to use a task. This program does not administer the tests or collect their results.
